advisor_signals.live_tex_excerpt: This chapter presents tools for constructing synthetic neural controllers, coupling them to different mechanical models, and testing their behavior efficiently. Earlier controller development work in AnimatLab required substantial manual adaptation and parameter tuning, motivating a more flexible workflow for neuromechanical modeling. Building on established neural architectures and simulation software, this workflow requires interfaces that connect neural outputs with actuator commands and return mechanical measurements as sensory feedback. I developed graphical neural-modeling tools, simulation interfaces, and Python scripts that connect these capabilities to support controller construction and testing with human biomechanical models and BPA-actuated robot models.

advisor_signals.live_tex_excerpt: The first mechanical design consideration is to select artificial muscles that can meet the robot joints' torque requirements within the available space. The McKibben-style braided pneumatic actuators (BPAs) used here combine low mass, high force-to-weight ratio, and intrinsic compliance with a force--length curve that qualitatively resembles that of skeletal muscle \citep{liang_comparative_2020, hunt_modeling_2017}. Our initial work with Festo BPAs showed that at shorter resting (uninflated) lengths, they delivered less force and contraction than what the manufacturer specifies. Existing empirical models describe useful pressure--contraction relationships \citep{sarosi_comparative_2017, martens_modeling_2017, hunt_modeling_2017}, but did not capture this relationship between resting length and force output. Therefore, I built a jig to perform isometric force experiments with Festo BPAs and collect data to further characterize this relationship. This data enabled the development of actuator force models that account for resting length, pressure, and contraction. The work in Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles} describes this process and the developed model.

advisor_signals.reason: Shortens the opening of the assembled-joint problem.
advisor_signals.live_tex_excerpt: The next mechanical design consideration is predicting joint torque of an assembled robot. When an artificial muscles pulls on a limb segment, it creates torque about the joint. This torque is what moves the body through space, causing the limbs to interact with objects and the ground. The artificial muscle force is transmitted to the skeleton through mounting brackets and artificial tendons. Brackets and fixtures can deflect under load, tendons can stretch, and contact with the skeleton bends an actuator. All this changes the force and torque that an artificial muscle applies to the limb. This compliance and actuator bending can therefore cause rigid-body predictions of torque typically used in robotic models to differ from actual torque. Initial tests showed that joint torque and the usable range of motion (RoM) on a knee joint were lower than predicted. I therefore built an isometric knee-torque test jig to develop a model of how the artificial muscle interacts with limb, and better predict the expected joint torque. The improved model was then used to design and test artificial musculotendon routes that can meet or exceed their human-muscle torque equivalents. The details of this process are described in (Chapter~\ref{ch:torque}).

When an artificial muscles pulls on a limb segment, it creates torque about the joint. This torque is what moves the body through space, causing the limbs to interact with objects and the ground. The artificial muscle force is transmitted to the skeleton through mounting brackets and artificial tendons. Brackets and fixtures can deflect under load, tendons can stretch, and contact with the skeleton bends an actuator. All this changes the force and torque that an artificial muscle applies to the limb. This compliance and actuator bending can therefore cause rigid-body predictions of torque typically used in robotic models to differ from actual torque. Initial tests showed that joint torque and the usable range of motion (RoM) on a knee joint were lower than predicted. I therefore built an isometric knee-torque test jig to develop a model of how the artificial muscle interacts with limb, and better predict the expected joint torque. The improved model was then used to design and test artificial musculotendon routes that can meet or exceed their human-muscle torque equivalents. The details of this process are described in (Chapter~\ref{ch:torque}).

paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models
paragraph_outputs.input: This chapter presents tools for constructing synthetic neural controllers, coupling them to different mechanical models, and testing their behavior efficiently. Earlier controller-transfer work in AnimatLab required substantial manual adaptation and parameter tuning, motivating a more flexible workflow for neuromechanical modeling. Building on established neural architectures and simulation software, this workflow requires interfaces that translate neural outputs into actuator commands and return mechanical measurements as sensory feedback. Graphical, block-based programming supports the construction and inspection of neural circuits and their signal paths, while headless simulation enables repeated experiments and automated parameter tuning without continuous interaction with a graphical interface. I developed graphical neural-modeling tools, simulation interfaces, and Python scripts that connect these capabilities to support controller construction and testing with human biomechanical models and BPA-actuated robot models.

paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models / Introduction: The Controller-Transfer Problem
paragraph_outputs.input: A neural controller acts through the mechanics to which it is connected. Changing muscle attachments, joint motion, inertia, or actuator behavior changes the mechanical response to a command and the sensory signals returned to the circuit. A controller that produces alternating motor activity can therefore fail to coordinate loading when transferred to a different body. Investigating that transfer requires tools that make the mechanical assumptions, neural computations, and exchanged signals accessible to inspection and controlled testing.

paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models / Introduction: The Controller-Transfer Problem
paragraph_outputs.input: An early experiment illustrated this problem. For a course project in ME 610: Neuromechanical Modeling, Morrow and I coupled the bipedal mechanics of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} with the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} in AnimatLab \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. The model included bilateral thigh, shank, foot, and toe segments, sagittal-plane joints, and antagonist Hill-type muscles. I added a passive toe joint. A shared rhythm generator (RG) supplied pattern-formation (PF) and motor-neuron (MN) pathways on both sides. We adjusted currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters manually and presented the suspended result at the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. The legs cycled when suspended, but the model lost support when released toward the ground (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}). The continued neural rhythm did not establish an effective load-bearing controller.

paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models / Introduction: The Controller-Transfer Problem
paragraph_outputs.input: This experience exposed a practical gap between assembling a neuromechanical model and using it to investigate control. Manual tuning made it difficult to isolate a faulty pathway, distinguish a mechanical error from a neural error, or reproduce a useful condition. Graphical construction could make circuits easier to inspect, while scripted execution could make parameter searches and repeated experiments practical. Both required explicit command and sensory interfaces, checked model mechanics, and evaluation criteria appropriate to the task.

paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models / Introduction: The Controller-Transfer Problem
paragraph_outputs.input: This chapter addresses the fourth dissertation objective by developing tools for constructing and testing coupled neural and mechanical models. The methods connect OpenSim- and CAD-derived mechanics, graphical neural construction, actuator and sensory interfaces, staged calibration, and automated experiments. The results proceed from mechanical and circuit checks to coupled responses, controlled interventions, and computational performance. OpenSim, MyoConverter, MuJoCo, SNS-Toolbox, Simulink, and Simscape provide the existing software foundations \citep{delp_opensim_2007,caggiano_myosuite_2022,todorov_mujoco_2012,nourse_sns_2023}. My contributions are the model preparation and repairs, editable blocks, actuator integrations, and experiment procedures that connect those foundations. Appendix~\ref{app:simulation_verification} gives supporting configurations, source scripts, and secondary comparisons.

paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models / Methods: Constructing and Evaluating Neuromechanical Models / Workflow and Experimental Models
paragraph_outputs.input: The workflow begins with a mechanical model and a control hypothesis (Figure~\ref{fig:simulation_workflow}). Model preparation establishes the coordinates, actuator routes, force calculations, and contacts through which neural activity will act. Controller construction defines the computations performed by neural populations and the signals they exchange. Calibration selects parameters for those functions, and physical evaluation tests the resulting coupled behavior. Recordings then connect changes in the circuit to changes in movement and loading. A failed test can require revising an earlier component before repeating the coupled experiment.

paragraph_outputs.input: Mechanical checks preceded controller fitting. Single-actuator tests checked action directions and force scales. paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models / Methods: Constructing and Evaluating Neuromechanical Models / Preparing the Mechanical Models
paragraph_outputs.input: The CAD route additionally required consistent anatomical frames, mass and inertia assignment, joint topology, and actuator attachments. The robot frame uses $x$ anterior, $y$ superior, and $z$ right. CAD assembly placement was related to that frame through a reference datum. The four-bar knees require their loop constraints to be retained in the dynamic model. Moving and conditional muscle-route points require both geometric updates and the corresponding force derivatives; changing a route's length without accounting for that dependence would give inconsistent generalized forces. Numerical derivative and virtual-work checks test those relations before interpreting motion.

paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models / Methods: Constructing and Evaluating Neuromechanical Models / Preparing the Mechanical Models
paragraph_outputs.input: Model preparation also includes declaring the actuation approximation. The implemented BPA interface evaluates the quasi-static force relationship from Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles} at current actuator length and commanded pressure, then applies tensile force along its route. This calculation carries the measured static force dependence into a neuromechanical experiment. Valve flow, pressure transients, and loading-history effects require additional models and calibration. Biological tendon compliance and BPA series compliance are likewise separate mechanisms. Selecting one of these implementations does not establish the fidelity of another.

paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models / Methods: Constructing and Evaluating Neuromechanical Models / Constructing Controllers and Closing the Feedback Loop
paragraph_outputs.input: The SNS-Simscape library implements neurons, chemical synapses, sensory encoders, activation dynamics, and muscle-force elements as editable Simulink blocks (Figure~\ref{fig:simulink_sns_implementation}). It retains the conductance-based formulations used by SNS-Toolbox \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Synapses supply conductance and conductance--reversal-potential products; the postsynaptic neuron combines these with its membrane state and other currents. Membrane voltage and normalized motor command remain distinct signals. This organization permits inspection of individual pathways and the calculations they perform.

paragraph_outputs.input: The complete feedback loop connects MN output to activation or a pressure command, the actuator model to tensile force, and the mechanical state to sensory encoding. Length, lengthening velocity, and force provide inputs for Ia, II, and Ib pathways; foot contact supplies a distinct event or load signal. Their encoding ranges, signs, saturation, and update intervals must be stated. A synaptic conductance is not itself a sensory force, and a normalized neural output is not a pressure until the command mapping defines that conversion. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_signal_contracts} records these interface distinctions.

Each test retains its actual integration settings.

paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models / Methods: Constructing and Evaluating Neuromechanical Models / Functional Design, Neural Calibration, and Physical Curriculum
paragraph_outputs.input: Functional design specifies what a neural pathway should compute before its parameters are fitted. The specification includes the represented quantity, input and output units, sign, operating range, temporal response, and saturation. For a PF channel, this includes the intended onset, duration, and overlap of its transmitted activity. A channel's flexor, extensor, or synergy label does not establish those properties. Graded and spiking realizations require design relationships appropriate to their respective neuron formulations; the equations and spiking calibration are given in Appendix~\ref{app:neuron_equations}.

paragraph_outputs.section: Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models / Methods: Constructing and Evaluating Neuromechanical Models / Functional Design, Neural Calibration, and Physical Curriculum
paragraph_outputs.input: Neural calibration then selects parameters for these declared functions. I implemented the four operations presented by \citet{hunt_inrc_2019}: establish an intrinsic rhythm with a period approximately twice the target locomotor period; tune entrainment using expected afferent signals; fit feedforward motor recruitment; and refine the motor pattern with sensory feedback. Expected activation targets are inverse-mechanics estimates from reference motion, rather than measured electromyograms. Their agreement with MN output measures the stated calibration target, not biological validation of every neural pathway.

Fitting therefore supports the physical curriculum rather than replacing it. The experiment drivers separately evaluate saved settings so that advancement can be checked without changing the candidate during the test.

paragraph_outputs.section: Appendix D: Supplementary Neuromechanical Verification
paragraph_outputs.input: This appendix provides the configuration details and secondary tests supporting Chapter~\ref{ch:sns}. paragraph_outputs.input: The conversion workflow involved two distinct problems: importing the robot's artificial-muscle routing with human muscle parameters, and repairing the converted human reference used for controller development. paragraph_outputs.section: Motivation
paragraph_outputs.input: The first mechanical design consideration is to select artificial muscles that can meet the robot joints' torque requirements within the available space. The McKibben-style braided pneumatic actuators (BPAs) used here combine low mass, high force-to-weight ratio, and intrinsic compliance with a force--length curve that qualitatively resembles that of skeletal muscle \citep{liang_comparative_2020, hunt_modeling_2017}. Our initial work with Festo BPAs showed that at shorter resting (uninflated) lengths, they delivered less force and contraction than what the manufacturer specifies. Existing empirical models describe useful pressure--contraction relationships \citep{sarosi_comparative_2017, martens_modeling_2017, hunt_modeling_2017}, but choosing actuator lengths required evaluating how resting length affects their output. Therefore, I built a jig to perform isometric force experiments with Festo BPAs. This allowed the development of force models that account for resting length, pressure, and contraction. The work in Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles} provides a basis for actuator sizing within the tested isometric conditions.

paragraph_outputs.section: Motivation
paragraph_outputs.input: The next mechanical design consideration is predicting joint torque of an assembled robot over the required knee motion. A robot knee transmits actuator force to the skeleton through mounting brackets and artificial tendons. Brackets and fixtures can deflect under load, tendons can stretch, and contact with the knee bends an actuator and changes its usable length. Differences between nominal and effective musculotendon length, series compliance, and actuator bending can therefore cause rigid-body predictions to differ from measured torque. Initial tests showed that joint torque and the usable range of motion (RoM) could be lower than predicted. I therefore built an isometric knee-torque test jig to develop correction factors, progressing from pinned-knee configurations to the biomimetic four-bar knee. The improved model was then used to design and test musculotendon routes against selected human-muscle torque targets (Chapter~\ref{ch:torque}).
paragraph_outputs.recorded_live_proposed_paragraph: The next mechanical design consideration is predicting joint torque of an assembled robot. When an artificial muscles pulls on a limb segment, it creates torque about the joint. This torque is what moves the body through space, causing the limbs to interact with objects and the ground. The artificial muscle force is transmitted to the skeleton through mounting brackets and artificial tendons. Brackets and fixtures can deflect under load, tendons can stretch, and contact with the skeleton bends an actuator. All this changes the force and torque that an artificial muscle applies to the limb. This compliance and actuator bending can therefore cause rigid-body predictions of torque typically used in robotic models to differ from actual torque. Initial tests showed that joint torque and the usable range of motion (RoM) on a knee joint were lower than predicted. I therefore built an isometric knee-torque test jig to develop a model of how the artificial muscle interacts with limb, and better predict the expected joint torque. The improved model was then used to design and test artificial musculotendon routes that can meet or exceed their human-muscle torque equivalents. The details of this process are described in (Chapter~\ref{ch:torque}).

paragraph_outputs.section: Motivation
paragraph_outputs.input: The first neural control design consideration is selecting sensory feedback pathways and defining how they influence a synthetic nervous system. Neural control architectures are often presented as schematic diagrams resembling flowcharts. These diagrams simplify biological neural circuits by showing selected connections and functional relationships, while implementing those relationships requires information about the pathways, their effects, and the conditions under which they operate. Therefore, it was necessary to gather and curate documented sensory pathways and rules describing how sensory input influences neural activity and movement, relying on computational models, animal experiments, and literature reviews. These findings are distributed across species, preparations, and experimental protocols, so their interpretation requires preserving the context in which they were reported \citep{van_de_crommert_review_1998, windhorst_muscle_2007, windhorst_spinal_2022}. The Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) was developed to organize this information into a searchable resource linked to its sources. The work in Chapter~\ref{ch:database} supports the selection of feedback pathways and the definition of biologically informed interactions in neuromechanical models.
paragraph_outputs.recorded_live_proposed_paragraph: In addition to the accurate biomechanical model of the human body, the goals of the bipedal robot project include the use of an underlying neural controller that mimics the human nervous system.  To build such a model, it is necessary to gather and curate a collection of material on how the nervous system is organized and how sensory input influences neural activity and movement. Unfortunately, there is not a complete understanding of this, no comprehensive view has been written or collected from scientific papers. Our understanding of neural control is distributed across species, preparations, and experimental protocols \citep{van_de_crommert_review_1998, windhorst_muscle_2007, windhorst_spinal_2022}. Therefore, I developed the Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) to aid in organizing the literature on the subject into a searchable resource linked to its sources. Chapter~\ref{ch:database} provides an overview of how the SADb was developed, how it is organized, and features that can be used to sort and understand the underlying material.
